title: He touched his ear (Luke 22:47–53)
hook: a disciple strikes a servant with a sword; Jesus heals the man's ear

segments.voice: Yesterday, agonia, sweat like drops of blood, and a prayer for the cup to pass. Your line was an angel strengthened him. What gave you strength to go through something? Day five hundred eighty-one.

Night on the Mount of Olives. Jesus is still speaking when a crowd arrives, and walking in front of them is Judas. He comes close to kiss Jesus. And Jesus asks him, quietly, in the King James words: "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?" The disciples see what's happening. Someone asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? And before anyone answers, one of them swings. The blade catches the high priest's servant and cuts off his right ear. Now there's blood on the ground, swords drawn in the dark, a crowd of armed men, and everything about to get worse.

Then Jesus speaks. The King James has: "Suffer ye thus far." The Greek is just a few words, and translators aren't sure exactly how to put them. Some render it let them have their way. Others say something like, no more of this, or enough. Either way, it's a word to stop. And then a detail only Luke tells. "And he touched his ear, and healed him." Hold that picture. Jesus is being arrested. His friends are panicking. He's about to be taken away to a night of trials and beatings. And in the middle of his own arrest, he heals a man from the side that came to take him. Not one of his own. A servant on the other side, bleeding in the dark. John's Gospel adds two names: the swordsman was Peter, and the servant was Malchus. Luke leaves them unnamed, and the scene works either way. Then Jesus turns to the chief priests and temple captains and elders who came out. You came with swords and clubs, as if I were a robber. I was with you every day in the temple, and you didn't lift a hand. "But this is your hour, and the power of darkness." Christians have gone back to this scene when they argue about violence and faith. Some hear in it a call to refuse force entirely. Others hear a limit on it. Both start from what Jesus did with his hands.

then, large: `AND HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: heal something you broke. Settle, and breathe. Think back over this week, or this year. Is there something you damaged in a moment of heat? A sharp text. A door slammed. A friendship you cut with one swing. Picture it plainly, without beating yourself up. Then picture one small thing that would begin to mend it. An apology. A call. Paying for what you broke. If you pray, you can ask God for the courage to do it. If you don't, just choose the first step. The bell holds the time.
Malchus. The high priest's servant whose ear Peter cut off and Jesus healed, named only in John's Gospel, not Luke's.

Your line: no more of this. This week took us from the end of the age to the upper room, the table, the garden and the arrest. Today, take one step to mend something you broke. Day five hundred eighty-one, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians remember the arrest during Holy Week, and some churches, such as the historic peace churches, return to scenes like this one when they teach about nonviolence.

fork.setup: you're in the garden. a friend has just cut off the ear of a man who came to arrest you. swords are out. what do you do?
options: stop the fight and heal the man's ear.
fork.reveal: "suffer ye thus far. and he touched his ear, and healed him." the healing is for the man on the other side.

original.note: Greek: the ear, especially the outer ear. the word Luke uses when Jesus touches and heals it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a disciple defends Jesus, and Jesus fixes the damage.
what it means: Jesus stops the violence and heals a man from the side that came to arrest him.
what a scholar hears: 'suffer ye thus far' renders a short, unclear Greek phrase, and only Luke reports the healing; John supplies the names Peter and Malchus.

notes: KJV 22:51 begins 'Suffer ye thus far'; the Greek (ἐᾶτε ἕως τούτου) is debated. The carry 'no more of this' follows modern renderings. Confirm.
'The last miracle of healing before the cross' in Luke: confirm no later healing in Luke's passion account.
The kiss as a customary greeting between disciple and teacher: common commentary. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Luke has no torches or olive grove (torches are John 18:3), so the hook now says night on the Mount of Olives; cut the unsourced 'ordinary greeting between student and teacher', 'a man screaming', the superlative 'last miracle of healing before the cross' (teach, word, myth, trapdoor), 'many modern versions', 'every version agrees' and 'all of them notice'; added the parallels behind 'only Luke tells' to sources.
